meta.scope_note: 29,787 intake-outcome records from Long Beach Animal Care Services covering 2017-01-01 to 2024-12-31. The data straddles a major operational pivot (Compassion Saves, May 2019), a global pandemic, and a record-breaking 2024.

det_01.label: Origin: City of Long Beach Animal Care Services
det_01.content: The dataset comes from the City of Long Beach Animal Care Services (LBACS), a municipal department that runs the open-admission shelter at the P.D. Pitchford Companion Animal Village inside El Dorado Park. LBACS serves Long Beach plus the contracted cities of Cerritos, Signal Hill, Los Alamitos, and Seal Beach, which is why the jurisdiction column contains those names. The TidyTuesday release on 2025-03-04 was curated by Lydia Gibson and surfaced via Emil Hvitfeldt's {animalshelter} R package; the underlying public records live on the City's open-data portal. Each row is one animal-stay: an intake event paired with an eventual outcome (adoption, rescue transfer, euthanasia, return-to-owner, etc.).

det_02.label: The Compassion Saves pivot (May 2019)
det_02.content: On 8 May 2019 the Long Beach City Council voted 8-0 to formally adopt the 'Compassion Saves' service model, replacing the older 'no-kill' framing with a philosophy that emphasises community outreach, supportive services, foster networks, and education over a single euthanasia threshold. The pivot followed years of advocacy and at least one task force after activist accusations that the shelter was killing treatable animals — including, as task force member Anna Wong told the Long Beach Post, kittens with as little as 3-5 percent body mange. By the end of 2019 LBACS reported a 33% drop in euthanasia versus 2018 and an 88% combined dog-cat save rate. This date is a structural break in the dataset: 2017 and most of 2018 reflect the pre-Compassion shelter; 2019 onward reflects the new model.

det_03.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
det_03.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. The reasoning is empirical, not ideological — Best Friends estimates that no more than ~10% of incoming cats and dogs have irreparable medical or behavioural conditions that prevent rehoming, so a well-run shelter should be able to save the rest. Live-release rate definitions vary slightly by jurisdiction (some include or exclude wildlife, owner-requested euthanasia, or animals dead-on-arrival), which is why interpretation matters when comparing LBACS to other systems. As of early 2025, more than two-thirds of U.S. shelters meet the 90% benchmark.

sources.title: What Is No-Kill? — The 90% Save Rate Benchmark — Best Friends
facts: A 90% save rate over 12 months is the benchmark for no-kill status
No more than ~10% of incoming dogs and cats are estimated to have irreparable medical/behavioural issues
More than 2 of 3 U.S. shelters reached no-kill in 2025

det_04.label: Trap-Neuter-Return is a population intervention, not a rescue
det_04.content: Roughly one in twenty rows in this dataset has the outcome 'shelter, neuter, return' or 'trap, neuter, release' — both are TNR programs in which a community cat is sterilised, vaccinated, ear-tipped, and returned to the location it came from rather than placed for adoption. Peer-reviewed work from the University of Florida and others shows targeted TNR can drop shelter cat intake by ~66% and cat euthanasia by 83-91% over multi-year horizons, because preventing kittens never born is far more efficient than processing them once they arrive. In the LBACS data, TNR outcomes look like 'releases' but are best read as a cat-population strategy: an animal exits the shelter alive, the colony shrinks over time, future intake falls. Reading those rows as 'lost' or 'released to the wild' would mislead the reader.

det_05.label: Why the pandemic dented intake, not adoptions
det_05.content: Across the U.S., shelter intake fell ~20.5% from 2019 (5.36M dogs and cats) to 2020 (4.26M) and stayed depressed in 2021. The drop was concentrated in stray intake — 172,070 strays in 2019 vs 123,540 in 2020 — because stay-at-home orders meant fewer humans wandering around to find loose animals, and non-emergency interstate transports paused. Adoptions, in contrast, held up or even surged in 2020 as people in lockdown bonded with pets. The widely repeated story that 'pandemic pets' were dumped en masse in 2022 has been fact-checked and is largely false; what really happened was that intake rebounded to near-pre-pandemic levels while adoption infrastructure (volunteers, foster networks) was still catching up. The LBACS data shows this textbook pattern: intakes collapsed in 2020-2021, then climbed back.

det_06.label: 2024: highest adoption rate ever
det_06.content: On 9 January 2025 the City of Long Beach announced LBACS had hit its 'highest adoption rate ever' in 2024 and surpassed the 1,500-pet placement target set by the 2024 strategic plan by approximately 500 animals. The figure cited in the press release for 2022 — 1,968 placements — already represented a 194% rise from 687 placements in 2018. The 2022 toolkit included a 'Compassion Saves' framework, a fleet 'Adoption Waggin' that ran 40+ offsite events, a Foster Coordinator role placing ~500 animals in homes, themed events ('Howl-O-Ween', 'Happy Howlidays'), and donation partnerships with Bixby Animal Clinic, Paw Shoppe Pet Center, Pet Supplies Plus, Zoom Room, and Pizzamania. Mayor Rex Richardson framed the gain as the payoff of community engagement and offsite events. The dataset's last row is 31 December 2024, so it covers the entire victory lap.

det_07.label: Naming convention: the asterisk means staff-named
det_07.content: Per the data dictionary, an animal_name beginning with '*' was assigned by shelter staff because the animal arrived without a known name (a stray, a wildlife pickup, an owner surrender who was not named in the paperwork). Blank animal_name fields mean the name was unknown and not assigned. This is more than a footnote: in 29,787 records, 9,965 names start with '*' and 12,162 are blank, leaving only ~7,660 animals (26%) who entered the shelter with a name their human had given them. The asterisk column is a quiet measure of attachment-at-intake, and a strong correlate of intake_type (owner-surrender vs stray vs wildlife).

det_08.label: Open-admission means the shelter takes anything that breathes
det_08.content: LBACS is open-admission and municipally contracted, which means it cannot turn animals away the way some private rescues can. That explains why the dataset's animal_type column is wider than 'cat' and 'dog' — it includes 2,075 birds, 1,412 'wild' animals (raccoons, opossums, skunks, coyotes, hawks), 526 rabbits, 344 reptiles, 172 guinea pigs, 10 livestock, and 3 amphibians. Wildlife typically enters under intake_type='wildlife' (4,473 rows) and exits via 'return to wild habitat', 'rescue' to a wildlife partner, or 'euthanasia' (when injuries are non-survivable). Reading wildlife outcomes by the same yardstick as cat/dog outcomes is a category error — the policy goals and ethical baselines are different.

det_09.label: Intake conditions encode triage, not just health
det_09.content: The intake_condition factor — 'normal', 'under age/weight', 'ill mild/moderate/severe', 'injured mild/moderate/severe', 'fractious', 'feral', 'aged', 'behavior moderate/severe', 'welfare seizures', 'i/i report' — is the shelter's triage code at the door. 'Under age/weight' (6,590 rows) overwhelmingly means neonatal kittens too young to survive without a nursing queen; nationally these animals are the single largest euthanasia category at open-admission shelters and the population that bottle-feeding foster networks were built to save. 'Fractious' usually means a cat too unsocialised to be handled (a candidate for TNR rather than adoption). Triage status at intake is a stronger predictor of outcome than species or age alone.

sources.title: Long Beach Animal Care Services

det_10.label: Geography: shelter is in El Dorado Park; intakes cluster downtown
det_10.content: The shelter itself sits at the P.D. Pitchford Companion Animal Village inside El Dorado Park East (~33.81N, -118.10W). Intake crossings, however, are scattered across the City of Long Beach, with the densest clusters in North Long Beach (90805, 90806), Downtown / West Long Beach, and parts of Wilmington/Carson border tracts. Cerritos and Signal Hill rows are the contracted-jurisdiction overflow. The latitude/longitude columns describe where the animal was found or surrendered, not where it ended up — useful for mapping intake hotspots, less useful for adoption geography.

det_11.label: What this analysis should focus on
det_11.content: Given the structure of the data and the external context, the strongest narrative spine runs along three axes: (1) the macro time-trend — pre-Compassion (2017-2018), the new-model years (2019), the pandemic dip (2020-2021), and the recovery / record (2022-2024); (2) species and triage-class outcome divergence — what happens to a 'normal' adult dog vs an 'under-age' kitten vs a 'wild' raccoon vs a 'fractious' community cat; (3) the human-attachment signal — owner-named vs star-named vs blank, length-of-stay, return-to-owner rates by intake type. Comparisons to the 90% save-rate benchmark and the city's own 1,500-placement strategic-plan target give the reader external anchors. Avoid causal language — the dataset cannot prove Compassion Saves caused the trend, only that the trend coincides with the policy.
